content: In November 2021, the FAO-WHO-WOAH tripartite convened a virtual Global Technical Meeting on MERS-CoV and other emerging zoonotic coronaviruses. This meeting included participants from affected and at-risk countries, academia, research institutions, partner organizations, donors, and other stakeholders. The meeting provided an opportunity to review the global MERS situation, assess the impact of the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, and discuss ways to resume and integrate preparedness and response activities for MERS. In September 2022, WHO officials conducted a technical mission to Saudi Arabia to evaluate the MERS situation in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic. This mission reviewed the impact of COVID-19 on MERS surveillance, preparedness, and response activities. Field sites were visited, and recommendations were made to strengthen surveillance, preparedness, and response systems. Collaborative efforts between WHO and Saudi Arabia, including the role of the Public Health Authority as a WHO Collaborating Center for MERS, were discussed and agreed upon. The Eastern Mediterranean Regional Office (EMRO) has developed an operational framework for integrated respiratory disease surveillance, prioritizing MERS as one of the viruses to be included in existing influenza sentinel surveillance systems. WHO continues to support field-based epidemiological studies at the animal-human interface to evaluate the extent of MERS-CoV infection in individuals with occupational exposure to dromedary camels. Since July 2019, studies have been completed in Pakistan and Somalia in collaboration with Ministries of Health and other technical partners. WHO is working with Ministries of Health in affected and at-risk countries, as well as international partners, to better understand MERS-CoV transmission patterns and risk factors in community and healthcare settings. The organization is also focused on developing improved measures to prevent human infections. Despite a reduction in human case detection, MERS-CoV continues to circulate in dromedary camels across large parts of the Middle East and Africa. WHO’s global risk assessment of MERS remains unchanged since the last publication in July 2019. Since early 2020, epidemiological surveillance activities have been prioritized for COVID-19, leading to reduced testing and detection of MERS cases. The non-specific nature of MERS symptoms complicates surveillance, often resulting in missed early cases, including index cases of spillover events. This creates opportunities for human-to-human transmission in healthcare settings. WHO continues to recommend and work with Member States and partners to emphasize the importance of improving standard infection prevention and control (IPC) measures in all healthcare facilities. It remains unclear which exposures result in virus transmission in healthcare settings or the role of environmental contamination in such transmissions. Studies from South Korea have identified MERS-CoV on surfaces in patient rooms and on equipment during patient stays and after discharge or death, highlighting the importance of adequate cleaning and disinfection. WHO encourages routine full genome sequencing when cases are identified in humans in contact with dromedary camels, as well as during clusters of cases or outbreaks in human populations. Sporadic introductions of MERS-CoV from dromedary camels into the human population in the Middle East continue to occur. Detection of secondary human-to-human transmission in healthcare and household settings has been noticeably reduced. However, large outbreaks in Jeddah/Riyadh in 2014, South Korea in 2015, and Riyadh in 2015 demonstrate that MERS-CoV can cause explosive outbreaks with significant health and socio-economic consequences if not adequately controlled. Human-to-human transmission and large outbreaks of MERS can be prevented with early suspicion, case isolation, and clinical management. Until zoonotic transmission from infected dromedary camels to humans is halted, the risk of human infections, particularly in healthcare settings, remains. WHO advocates for the development of dromedary vaccines to prevent human infection and is committed to better understanding the geographic extent of MERS-CoV infection in dromedary camels and human populations, as well as the spillover risk. Studies at the dromedary camel-human interface are being funded in several countries in Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia. During the FAO-WHO-WOAH Global Technical Meeting on MERS-CoV and other emerging zoonotic coronaviruses in 2021, experts suggested that MERS-CoV recombination with SARS-CoV-2 is a remote possibility. Field investigations into this possibility are underway, and surveillance systems should be established to detect recombinants in areas where both viruses circulate. Control of MERS-CoV, like other zoonotic coronaviruses, requires national leadership, coordination between animal and human sectors using a One Health approach, public trust, and clear communication to healthcare facilities on measures to limit human-to-human transmission. Thorough investigation of all cases and rapid dissemination of knowledge gained during outbreak investigations and research on MERS-CoV are essential. WHO is working closely with FAO and WOAH to better understand MERS-CoV dynamics at the animal-human interface through a One Health approach. While human-to-human transmission has been detected among close contacts of confirmed MERS patients, there is no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission in the community. The overall transmission patterns remain unchanged, with an R0 of less than 1. However, the R0 in healthcare-associated outbreaks is higher, as documented in Saudi Arabia and South Korea. Early isolation of cases and adequate IPC measures can reduce the R0 to less than 1. Until more is understood about the mode of transmission and risk factors for infection, cases resulting from animal-to-human (zoonotic) transmission will continue to occur, potentially leading to limited community transmission and significant healthcare-associated outbreaks. Consistent application of adequate IPC measures has been used to end transmission in previous clusters. Investigations into exported cases who reported performing Umrah in Saudi Arabia revealed that all had visited healthcare facilities, come into contact with dromedary camels, or consumed raw camel products while in Saudi Arabia. WHO has developed a roadmap for the R&D of MERS-specific diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccines. This includes an updated roadmap for MERS diagnostics in 2018 and a broader public health research agenda for MERS. WHO, FAO, and WOAH have repeatedly brought together technical partners to assess and advance research needed for MERS in dromedary populations, at the human-animal interface, and in human populations. The latest Global Technical Meeting on MERS-CoV and Other Emerging Zoonotic Coronaviruses, held virtually in November 2021, reviewed the global MERS situation, the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, and ways to integrate preparedness and response activities for MERS. Epidemiologic investigations into MERS-CoV transmission patterns have been conducted and published, with more studies planned or underway. WHO expects the results of such investigations to be shared with affected countries and published promptly. Urgent research needs include understanding the natural history of MERS-CoV in dromedary camels, evaluating the risk of zoonotic transmission from camel products, improving surveillance to assess viral shedding, and accelerating vaccine development. At the animal-human interface, mapping virus circulation, evaluating spillover risks, and conducting serological and virological studies are critical. In human populations, research priorities include understanding risk factors for infection among healthcare workers, the role of asymptomatic cases, and the integration of MERS testing into respiratory disease surveillance systems. WHO emphasizes the importance of limiting the spread of infection in animal populations through vaccine development and better management of infected animals to reduce human exposure risk. Field-based studies at the animal-human interface are being supported to evaluate spillover risks in countries outside the Arabian Peninsula and Africa. Understanding transmission in healthcare settings, particularly the role of asymptomatic healthcare workers and environmental contamination, is urgently needed. Enhancing IPC awareness and implementation measures remains critical to preventing the spread of MERS-CoV in healthcare facilities. Early identification of MERS-CoV patients is challenging due to mild or non-specific symptoms, underscoring the importance of robust IPC measures in all healthcare settings.
